newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM ducks public eye as prosecutors decide.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM ducks public eye as prosecutors decide.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu kept out of the public eye, even cancelling two appearances, while waiting to hear on Sunday if prosecutors would charge him in a corruption scandal.
Ahead of an official announcement expected later in the day, all major Israeli newspapers and radio stations predicted Netanyahu would not be indicted.

But the reports said Netanyahu could face a rebellion from cabinet ministers who could topple his coalition government if the findings over the short-lived appointment in January of an attorney general raised serious questions about his integrity.

The scandal has cast a giant shadow over Middle East peacemaking, already in crisis since Netanyahu broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last month and sparked an outburst of violence.
"If mistakes were made here, they were routine political mistakes that were made by governments in the past," Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan told army radio.

Israel's state attorney Edna Arbel, after six days poring over a 995-page police recommendation to put Netanyahu on trial, told reporters on Sunday: "Everything's already signed and sealed." But she did not say what the conclusions were.
"I imagine that first of all, people who are involved must hear our decisions and afterwards the public will also know. The decision was hard and it's certainly not simple," she said.
"Judgment Day", the daily newspaper Maariv called it.

The 47-year-old Likud party leader, elected 11 months ago on a promise to pursue peace with security, last week became the first Israeli prime minister to face a police recommendation he be brought to trial -- on charges of fraud and breach of trust.
Police recommended the prime minister and three officials be indicted in connection with the appointment of Roni Bar-On, a lawyer and Likud activist, as attorney general three months ago.
Bar-On quit 12 hours after taking office amid strong public criticism that he was a legal lightweight unfit for the job.

Israel's Channel One television sparked the investigation by alleging that politician Aryeh Deri, a Netanyahu ally on trial for corruption, promoted Bar-On for the job in the hope of winning a plea bargain.
The television said Deri had promised that in return, his Shas party would support Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to pull back Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Police also recommended charges be brought against Deri, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi and the prime minister's director-general Avigdor Lieberman. All deny any wrongdoing.
Netanyahu, who has made a career of going before the cameras, stayed out of the limelight, putting off the two appearances he had scheduled for Sunday.
His office said he was too busy with other things.
"There will be consultations both on security and diplomatic issues and I am sure that the attorney general issue will come up as well," a spokeswoman said.
Netanyahu has described the influence-peddling scandal as "nonsense" and rejected calls to resign. If indicted, he would still be under no legal obligation to quit.

Yet even if he is not charged, a scathing report could prompt angry coalition partners to pull out, toppling Netanyahu's coalition of mainly right-wing and religious parties which holds 66 seats in the 120-member parliament.

"Even if no one is charged, should it become clear that very serious things were done from a public and democratic standpoint, we'll not be able to go on backing such a government and will want early elections," said Yehuda Harel of the four-member Third Way party in the coalition.
The Yisrael ba-Aliya party of Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky was also considering bolting the government if Netanyahu was charged or severely criticised. The party has seven legislators.
Even if Netanyahu is not indicted, the opposition can ask Israel's High Court of Justice to force charges to be brought based on the evidence.
